name: Deuteronomy
v:
Listen, sky — I'm about to speak.
Earth, catch every word from my mouth.

Let my teaching fall like rain,
my speech settle like dew,
like cloudbursts on tender grass,
like soaking showers on new growth.

I'm calling out the name of the LORD —
give our God the weight he deserves.

He is the Rock. His work is flawless.
Every path he walks is justice.
A God of faithfulness, no crookedness in him —
upright. True.

But his children? They wrecked it.
The corruption is theirs, not his —
a twisted, crooked generation.

Is this how you repay the LORD,
you fools, you brainless people?
Isn't he your Father, the one who bought you,
who made you and set you on your feet?

Remember the old days.
Think back through the generations.
Ask your father — he'll tell you.
Ask the elders — they'll explain.

When the Most High parceled out the nations,
when he split humanity into peoples,
he drew the borders
according to the number of the divine sons.

But the LORD's share was his own people —
Jacob, the lot assigned to him.

He found him in a wasteland,
in a howling emptiness of desert.
He circled around him, watched over him,
guarded him like the pupil of his eye.

Like an eagle stirring its nest,
hovering above its young —
he spread his wings, caught him,
carried him on his pinions.

The LORD alone led him.
No foreign god alongside.

He set him riding high on the land,
fed him the produce of the fields,
nursed him with honey from the rock,
oil from the flint-stone cliffs,

curds from the herd, milk from the flock,
fat lambs, prize rams of Bashan,
goats, and the finest wheat —
and you drank wine, the blood of grapes, foaming red.

But Jeshurun grew fat — and kicked.
You got fat, bloated, stuffed —
and you abandoned the God who made you,
treated the Rock of your rescue like nothing.

You provoked him with foreign gods,
disgusted him with abominations.

You sacrificed to demons — not God —
to gods you'd never known,
newcomers just arrived on the scene,
gods your ancestors never feared.

The Rock who fathered you — you forgot him.
The God who labored to bring you forth — you blanked him out.

The LORD saw it and spurned them —
his own sons and daughters had provoked him.

He said: I'll hide my face from them.
I'll see what becomes of them.
Because they're a generation gone sideways,
children with no faithfulness in them.

They made me jealous with a no-god,
provoked me with their empty idols.
So I'll make them jealous with a no-people,
provoke them with a nation of fools.

A fire has blazed up in my anger —
it burns down to the deepest grave.
It consumes the earth and what it grows.
It scorches the foundations of the mountains.

I'll pile disasters on them.
I'll empty my quiver into them.

Wasted by hunger, devoured by plague,
ravaged by bitter destruction —
I'll send the fangs of beasts against them,
the venom of crawling things in the dust.

Outside, the sword will take their children.
Inside, the houses, terror —
young men, young women,
nursing babies, gray-haired elders.

I said: I'll scatter them to the wind.
I'll erase their memory from humankind.

Except — I dreaded the enemy's gloating,
dreaded their adversaries getting it wrong,
saying, "Our own hand did this.
The LORD had nothing to do with it."

These are a nation without sense,
no discernment in them.

If only they were wise — they'd see this.
They'd understand where it ends.

How could one chase a thousand,
two put ten thousand to flight,
unless their Rock had sold them out,
unless the LORD had handed them over?

Because their rock is not like our Rock —
even our enemies admit it.

Their vine grows out of Sodom's soil,
out of Gomorrah's fields.
Their grapes are poison.
Their clusters, bitter.

Their wine is serpent venom,
the deadly cruelty of cobras.

Isn't this stored up with me,
sealed away in my vaults?

Vengeance is mine. Repayment too.
In time, their foot will slip.
The day of their disaster is racing close.
What's coming for them is hurtling in fast.

The LORD will vindicate his people.
He'll show mercy to his servants
when he sees their strength is spent,
when no one is left — neither slave nor free.

He'll say: Where are their gods now?
The rock they ran to for shelter —

who ate the fat of their sacrifices,
drank the wine of their offerings?
Let them get up and help you.
Let them be your hiding place.

See it now — I, I am he.
There is no god beside me.
I kill and I bring to life.
I wound and I heal.
And no one can wrench anything from my hand.

I raise my hand to heaven and swear:
As I live forever —

when I sharpen my flashing sword,
when my hand grips justice,
I'll bring vengeance on my foes,
I'll repay those who hate me.

My arrows will drink blood till they're drunk,
my sword will devour flesh —
blood of the slain and the captive,
heads of the enemy commanders.

Celebrate, you nations, with his people!
For he avenges the blood of his servants,
brings vengeance down on his foes,
and cleanses his land, his people.
Moses came and spoke every word of this song in the hearing of the people — he and Joshua son of Nun.
When Moses finished reciting all these words to all Israel,
he said to them: Take to heart every word I've testified to you today. Command your children to keep them — to do every word of this Torah, carefully.
This is no empty thing for you. This is your life. By this word you'll live long in the land you're crossing the Jordan to possess.
That same day the LORD spoke to Moses:
Climb this mountain — the Abarim range, Mount Nebo, in Moab, across from Jericho. Look out over Canaan, the land I'm giving to the Israelites as their possession.
On that mountain you're climbing — you will die. You'll be gathered to your people, the way your brother Aaron died on Mount Hor and was gathered to his.
Because you both broke faith with me among the Israelites at the waters of Meribah-Kadesh in the wilderness of Zin — you didn't treat me as holy among them.
You'll see the land from a distance. But you won't enter it — the land I am giving to the people of Israel.

com.d:
# Devotional Commentary on Deuteronomy 32

This final song of Moses reveals the heart of God as both covenant keeper and righteous judge—a stunning portrait of divine faithfulness tested by human unfaithfulness. Through ancient poetry, Moses calls Israel to remember that blessing and curse flow directly from the condition of their hearts toward God.

The song opens with an urgent summons: "Give ear, O heavens, and I will speak; and let the earth hear the words of my mouth" (32:1). Moses doesn't merely scold; he appeals to creation itself as witness to what unfolds between God and His people. He reminds them that the Lord is their Rock, their Father, their Creator—language that binds them in the deepest relational covenant. Yet this tenderness makes their abandonment all the more grievous. Israel's ingratitude isn't merely a breach of law; it's betrayal of a Father's love.

The heart of the passage acknowledges a painful truth: God's people will turn away. "They have acted corruptly toward him; to their shame they are no longer his children" (32:5). Yet even in describing this rebellion, Moses holds open a window to restoration. The song doesn't end in condemnation but in vindication—God's ultimate triumph and restoration of His people, even those who seem most lost.

This passage teaches that covenant with God isn't transactional but relational. Our unfaithfulness doesn't surprise God or catch Him unprepared; rather, it tests whether we truly believe He is worth our loyalty. The song invites us into honest reckoning: How have we acted corruptly toward our God? Where have we sought satisfaction in lesser things?

Yet the deepest invitation is to return. God's faithfulness never wavers, even when ours does. Moses' song assures us that our seasons of wandering don't define our destiny—our willingness to hear God's voice and turn back does.

What does returning to wholehearted devotion to God require of you today?
com.s:
Deuteronomy 32 presents the Song of Moses, a masterful poem that stands as one of the most sophisticated literary compositions in the Hebrew Bible. Delivered on the plains of Moab as Moses prepares Israel for his departure and their entry into Canaan, this covenant lawsuit (*rîb*) draws upon ancient Near Eastern treaty forms while transcending them theologically. The poem functions as a prophetic witness against future apostasy, explicitly commissioned by YHWH in the preceding chapter as testimony that will endure through generations of Israelite unfaithfulness and restoration.

The opening verses establish a cosmic courtroom by summoning heaven and earth as witnesses, a convention paralleled in Hittite suzerainty treaties where deities served as guarantors. The term *leqaḥ* ("teaching" or "doctrine") in verse 2 carries connotations of persuasive instruction that penetrates like rain into receptive soil, establishing the didactic intent of what follows. Central to the poem's theology is the designation of YHWH as *ṣûr* ("Rock"), appearing six times throughout the chapter. This metaphor emphasizes divine stability, reliability, and protective strength—qualities set in stark contrast to Israel's fickleness and the impotence of foreign deities, whose "rock" is explicitly deemed inferior in verse 31.

The poem's structure moves from theophanic praise through historical recollection of YHWH's election and nurture of Israel, to indictment of Israel's ingratitude and idolatry, then to announcement of judgment, and finally to promised vindication and restoration. The provocative theology of verses 8–9, where the Most High (*ʿElyôn*) distributes nations according to the number of divine beings while reserving Israel as YHWH's own inheritance, has generated substantial scholarly discussion. The Septuagint and Dead Sea Scrolls read "sons of God" (*bĕnê ʾĕlōhîm*) rather than the Masoretic "sons of Israel," suggesting an older textual tradition with implications for understanding Israelite monotheism's development within a divine council framework.

The poem concludes with YHWH's self-declaration of exclusive deity and sovereign power over life and death, culminating in a call for the nations to rejoice with God's people. This eschatological horizon transforms what begins as judgment into ultimate redemption, establishing patterns that later prophetic literature would develop extensively. The canonical placement of this song at the Pentateuch's conclusion provides Israel with both warning and hope as they stand perpetually at the threshold of promise.
com.p:
The Song of Moses stands at the threshold of Israel's entrance into Canaan, delivered approximately 1400 years before Christ's incarnation, in the final days of Moses' earthly ministry. This covenant lawsuit set to poetry arrives at a pivotal moment in redemptive history—the generation of the Exodus has perished in the wilderness, and their children now stand poised to inherit the promises made to Abraham six centuries earlier. The passage thus occupies that critical juncture between the Exodus and the Kingdom, when the seed of Abraham would finally possess the land flowing with milk and honey.

This prophetic song functions as a divine witness against Israel, written not merely to record history but to prophesy it. Moses, under inspiration, sees across the centuries—Israel's future apostasy, God's jealousy kindled by their idolatry, the scattering among nations, and ultimately, the vindication of God's servants and atonement for the land. The song traces the entire arc from Israel's election through judgment to final restoration, compressing millennia into verses.

The typological richness begins with Moses himself, who delivers this prophetic word yet cannot enter the land—a priest-prophet who leads God's people to the boundary but cannot complete the salvation. This shadows the insufficiency of the Law to bring God's people into final rest, awaiting the greater Prophet whom Moses foretold. The Rock appears throughout the song as Israel's foundation, the One who begot them, the Rock of their salvation—imagery the apostles would later apply directly to Christ, the spiritual Rock who accompanied Israel through the wilderness.

The passage prophesies Israel's provocation of God through "no-gods" and God's corresponding provocation of them through "no-people"—a prophecy Paul explicitly identifies as fulfilled in the ingathering of Gentiles into the covenant community. What Israel's unfaithfulness could not accomplish, God's faithfulness achieved through bringing jealousy upon His ancient people by grafting wild olive branches into the cultivated tree.

The eschatological horizon extends to the final day when God will avenge the blood of His servants and render vengeance to His adversaries. The song culminates in atonement for the land and people—language that points beyond animal sacrifice to the once-for-all offering that would cleanse not merely Israel's land but the entire creation.

For the church dwelling between the advents, this song declares that God's purposes cannot be thwarted by human unfaithfulness. The Rock remains unchanging, His arrows will find their mark, and the nations will ultimately rejoice with His people when redemption reaches its appointed consummation.
